Retry budget

What. How the crawler decides when to stop retrying a failed request. Answer. Each request gets three tries, and the third failure goes to the dead-letter table. Read this if you change the retry code or read a dead-letter alert.

1 · Why the budget exists

  1. The crawler used to retry a failed request until it worked.
  2. On 2026-09-14 one bad proxy pool turned that loop into 40,000 requests an hour against one account.
  3. A fixed budget stops that loop, so a broken upstream costs at most three calls per request.
  4. The worker counts tries in retry_count and gives up after the third one.
  5. We kept the count in the row and not in Redis, because a restart must not reset it.
flowchart LR
  R["Request fails"] --> C{"retry_count below 3?"}
  C -->|"yes"| W["Wait, then try again"]
  W --> R
  C -->|"no"| D["Write to dead_letters"]

2 · How a retry runs

  1. The worker waits before each new try, and the wait doubles each time.
  2. The first retry waits 10 seconds after the failure.
  3. The second retry waits 20 seconds and picks a different proxy pool.
  4. The third failure writes the request to dead_letters with the last status code.
  5. A longer wait did not help in the 2026-09 test, because a dead pool stays dead for hours.
TryWaitProxy
1nonesame pool
210 ssame pool
320 snew pool

3 · What an alert means

  1. An alert fires when more than 2% of an hour's requests reach the dead-letter table.
  2. At that rate the cause is almost always one upstream, so check the newest rows first.
  3. The status code on the newest rows names the upstream that broke.
  4. The owner put the rule this way: "three tries, then stop, then tell me."
  5. The waits between tries stay at 10–20 seconds.

The two numbers to watch are the 2% alert line and the 20-second last wait.
